column4: The section cites this three-class staging (أَزْوَاجًا ثَلَاثَةً) before the right and left groups; it makes the paired sides part of a larger reckoning scene.
The cited أصحاب الميمنة are named here as the people of the right; this is the section’s direct counterpart and positive pole.
The cited أصحاب المشأمة are named here as the people of the left; this is the section’s direct counterpart and negative pole.
After the two side groups, this scene names the third class, السابقون; it preserves the threefold staging that the section quotes at 56:7.
أصحاب اليمين restates the right-side group under the hand-name; this is the same community label in the section’s cited scene.
أصحاب الشمال restates the left-side group under the hand-name; this supplies the paired negative label from the same surah.
The person handed his book in his right hand introduces the successful side; the section specifically compares this hand assignment with its right-side people.
The right-hand recipient says he expected to meet his account (مُلَاقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ); the section contrasts this correct expectation with 90:5’s false assumption that no one has power over him.
The right-hand recipient’s pleasant life is the outcome that follows his book and expectation, making the side a lasting destination.
The right-hand recipient is placed in a high garden (جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ); it gives the section’s right-side destination a concrete setting.
The garden’s reachable clusters (قُطُوفُهَا دَانِيَةٌ) continue the right-hand recipient’s scene of settled reward.
The right-hand recipient is told to eat and drink for what he sent ahead; the scene ties his destination to prior deeds, as 90:17 ties the right-side group to faith and compassion.
The other person receives his book in his left hand; this is the direct opposite of the right-hand allotment used in the section.
The left-hand recipient wishes he had not received his book, the reverse of the right-hand speaker’s expectation at 69:20.
His wish that death had ended matters continues the left-hand recipient’s regret over judgment.
He says his wealth did not avail him; the failed worldly holding contrasts with the final side assigned by his record.
He says his authority has vanished; this continues the left-hand recipient’s loss of worldly standing at judgment.
The command to seize and bind him continues the same left-hand recipient’s transition from regret to punishment.
He is sent into the blazing Fire (الْجَحِيمَ); this gives the condemned side the fire destination that 90:20 names.
The punished man did not believe in God; this is a concrete counterpart to the side defined in 90:19 by denying God’s signs.
He did not urge feeding the poor (طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), reversing the feeding in famine that 90:14, 90:15, and 90:16 places among the acts preceding the right-side group.
The book is given in the right hand; this is another direct hand-assignment of the successful side named in the section.
The right-hand recipient receives an easy reckoning, continuing the reward attached to that hand assignment.
He returns to his people joyfully; this continues the right-hand scene with a concrete outcome.
The other person receives his book behind his back (وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ), a specific reversed placement paired with the right-hand book.
The behind-the-back recipient calls for destruction, continuing the regret of the section’s adverse side.
He enters the Blaze (سَعِيرًا); this locates the adverse book-receiving group in punishment.
At the gathering, the person given his book in his right hand reads it and is not wronged; this is another explicit link between the right hand and judgment by one’s record.
Two recorders sit on the right and left (عَنِ الْيَمِينِ وَعَنِ الشِّمَالِ); the judgment setting gives the paired directions a role before final group assignment.
The next ayah says no word is spoken without a watcher ready; it completes what the two recorders on either side receive, while this ayah itself supplies that paired placement.
The believers’ light runs before them and at their right sides (بِأَيْمَانِهِمْ); the section’s right-side association with a fortunate outcome is made visible as light.
Hypocrites ask to borrow the believers’ light, then a wall separates them with mercy inside and punishment outside; it develops the boundary implicit in the section’s two final sides.
The separated hypocrites ask believers whether they had not been with them; this continues the partition scene and makes group affiliation part of the division.
The hypocrites and disbelievers are told their refuge is the Fire; this completes the separation scene with the adverse destination.
Believers have reward and light, while disbelievers who deny the signs are أصحاب الجحيم; the verse joins the section’s right-light association to its denied-signs and fire side.
Every soul is held to what it earned except the people of the right (أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ); the exception directly establishes the side distinction.
The exception is named أصحاب اليمين, the very right-side community the section links to the coming exchange.
The right-side people are in gardens asking about criminals; this stages the parties whose exchange the section cites.
The right-side group asks about the criminals; this identifies who speaks across the divide.
They ask what brought the criminals into Saqar; the question makes the opposite group’s destination explicit.
The criminals say they were not among those who prayed; this begins their account of what led to their side.
They say they did not feed the poor (نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ), directly reversing 90:14, 90:15, and 90:16’s famine feeding and explaining the section’s use of this exchange.
They admit joining those who plunged into vain talk; this gives a concrete account of the company they kept on the condemned side.
They say they denied the Day of Judgment; this directly matches the rejection that marks the section’s adverse group.
They say certainty came to them; this closes the criminals’ account of reaching the opposite destination.

The sleepers are turned on their right and left sides (ذَاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ الشِّمَالِ); this is bodily orientation, not a moral group. It parallels the source section’s dictionary note about the dead being laid on the right, while the verse itself describes sleep.
At the coming Day, people divide into wretched and happy (شَقِيٌّ وَسَعِيدٌ); this echoes the section’s gloss of right as good fortune and left as ill fortune.
The wretched are in the Fire with groaning; it completes the adverse half of the division introduced at 11:105.
The Fire group remains there for the stated duration; this develops the section’s claim that the final side becomes a place of abiding.
The happy are in the Garden, abiding there; this completes the opposite destination and echoes the section’s fortunate right-side association.
The disbelievers are driven to Hell in groups; the scene makes a condemned community’s destination a place reached together.
They are told to enter Hell’s gates and abide there; it completes the left-like group’s destination as a lasting place.
Those who feared their Lord are driven to the Garden in groups; this sets the opposite community and route beside the Hell-bound group.
The Garden group says God fulfilled His promise and lets them settle in the Garden; this completes the positive side’s fixed destination.
Companions of the Garden call companions of the Fire across their different outcomes; the scene gives the section’s two side-communities a direct exchange.
The condemned are described as blocking God’s path and denying the Hereafter; this makes their road and refusal concrete beside the section’s two guided roads and denied signs.
A barrier lies between the Garden and Fire, with people on the heights; this renders the opposing destinations as a spatial boundary.
Those on the heights look toward the companions of the Fire; this continues the separated groups’ scene from a third position.
The people on the heights recognize men by their marks and address them; this gives the boundary scene distinct communities and visible affiliation.
The exchange at the heights turns toward entry into the Garden; this continues the question of who reaches which side.
Companions of the Fire ask Garden people for water and are refused; the scene makes the boundary and opposed destinations tangible.
Those who deny the signs are أصحاب النار and abide there; the phrase links the section’s companions of the adverse side to enduring residence.
Those who believe and do good are أصحاب الجنة and abide there; this is the positive counterpart to the Fire companions, supporting the section’s gloss of companions as those who remain attached.
The verse says the companions of Fire and Garden are not equal, then calls the Garden companions successful; it directly pairs enduring communities and opposite outcomes.
The surah opens by asking about the one who denies the Judgment; this is the denial that the section associates with the adverse side.
That denier repels the orphan; this gives another concrete reversal of the care that precedes the right-side label in 90.
He does not urge feeding the poor (طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), matching the section’s specific link between the condemned group and failure to feed.

The section identifies the root ق س م with dividing; this verse says God apportioned livelihoods among people (قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُمْ مَعِيشَتَهُمْ). It is a worldly allocation, not the two final sides, so the link is lexical and limited.

Hell has seven gates and each has an allotted portion (جُزْءٌ مَقْسُومٌ); the section’s q-s-m division of final groups has a specific afterlife parallel here, though this verse describes seven shares rather than two sides.
The threat says God would seize him بِالْيَمِينِ; the source section lists the dictionary sense yamin as strength, a forceful sense distinct from the blessed right-side title.
The heavens are folded بِـيَمِينِهِ; the source section’s dictionary form lists yamin as strength, while this verse speaks of divine dominion rather than human right-side groups.

The followers say leaders came to them عَنِ الْيَمِينِ; if this is heard in the source section’s secondary sense of force, it links right with power, though the verse’s phrase is interpretively uncertain and does not name a final side.
People call good fortune theirs but blame Moses for misfortune; the source section glosses yumn as blessing and شؤم as ill omen, while this ayah shows the ill-omen label being wrongly assigned.
Thamud say they take an omen from Salih and his followers, and he answers that their omen is with God; the section’s شؤم gloss meets a specific reversal of who bears misfortune.
The town’s people say the messengers are an ill omen for them; this is the accusation that the next ayah reverses, matching the section’s شؤم sense.
The messengers answer that their omen is with them; this completes the reversal and shows ill fortune as an attribution tied to the people’s own conduct.

All are brought into view with nothing concealed; this ayah introduces the public judgment scene before the next ayah assigns the book to the right hand, and it echoes the section’s challenged claim that no one sees.
The human is described as laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him; this opens the same book-and-destination scene with effort leading to encounter.
The person later handed his book behind his back had been joyful among his people; this gives the worldly stance that precedes his false expectation in the next ayah.
He thought he would never return to God; this is a specific false expectation opposite the right-hand recipient’s expectation in 69:20 and the section’s mistaken assumption in 90:5.
His Lord had been watching him; this completes the false-return scene and answers the section’s 90:7 question about whether anyone sees.

Each person’s lot or record is fastened to that person’s neck; the attachment concretely parallels the section’s gloss of أصحاب as those who stay attached to a side, though this ayah does not name either side.
The person is told to read his record and is his own reckoner; this completes the preceding image of an individual record attached to its bearer.

The scripture’s inheritors are divided into three moral classes, from those wronging themselves to those foremost in good; this is another concrete triad beside the section’s cited three classes in 56:7 and its two named sides.

Believers are brought from darkness into light, while disbelievers are brought from light into darkness and become lasting companions of the Fire; this joins the section’s right-light and adverse-side associations in a distinct paired formulation.

Those who disbelieve and deny the signs are companions of the Fire, abiding there; this closely restates the section’s denial-of-signs group and supports its gloss of companions as residents attached to a side.
Created shadows incline to the right and left while prostrating; this makes right and left tangible as directions, though the ayah describes shadows rather than human moral groups.
Iblis says he will sit against people on God’s straight path; this sets up the section’s image of guidance and chosen ways as a contest over direction.
Iblis says he will approach people from before, behind, right, and left; this is a hostile use of side-directions around the guided path, not the final two groups, and continues the preceding threat.
The one who gives and is mindful of God takes the favorable course; this parallels the compassionate good deeds preceding the right-side group.
The giver affirms the good; this makes the positive course a matter of belief as well as action.
God eases that person toward ease; the chosen course reaches a fitting end, clarifying the section’s road-to-destination image.
The opposing person withholds and feels self-sufficient; this reverses the generosity and humility associated with the favorable side.
That person denies the good; this parallels the denial that defines the section’s adverse group.
God eases the withholding denier toward hardship; this gives the other course its distinct destination.
His wealth will not avail when he falls; this gives a specific limit to worldly possession on the adverse course.
God declares that guidance is His responsibility; this frames the two courses in the preceding and following ayat as guidance.
The first life and the Hereafter belong to God; this completes the guidance frame with the final domain of the two courses.
The surah warns of a blazing Fire; this gives the adverse course a concrete end like the fire over the section’s left-side people.
Only the most wretched will burn in that Fire; this identifies the condemned class following the warning.
The condemned person denies and turns away; this concretely matches the rejection associated with the adverse side.
The most God-fearing are kept away from the Fire; this is the positive group’s explicit opposite outcome.
The God-fearing person gives wealth to purify himself; this links a concrete act of giving to the favorable end.
His giving is not repayment of another’s favor; this specifies the motive behind the positive course.
He seeks only his Lord’s countenance; this completes the motive of the giving.
He will be satisfied; this closes the positive course with its promised outcome.
Humanity is guided to a way, then becomes grateful or ungrateful; this directly links the section’s two guided roads with the two kinds of people who reach its sides.
For the ungrateful, the next ayah names chains, shackles, and a blaze; this gives the adverse road a concrete punishment.
The righteous are introduced with a drink of camphor; this begins the positive group’s reward scene.
The righteous fulfill vows and fear a day whose evil spreads widely; this describes the conduct and judgment-awareness of the positive group.
They give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite wanting it themselves; this is a direct parallel to the section’s feeding of the orphan and poor before the right-side label.
They say they feed only for God, seeking neither repayment nor thanks; this specifies the motive of the compassionate act.
They fear a severe day from their Lord; this continues the good group’s stance toward the judgment that divides the sides.
God protects them from that day’s evil and gives them joy; this supplies the outcome of their stance.
Their patience is rewarded with a Garden and silk; this completes the positive group’s path with a lasting place.
Those whose scales are heavy receive a favorable outcome; this is a measured division of people into distinct final conditions.
The heavy-scaled person is in a pleasing life; this gives the favorable side a lived destination.
Those whose scales are light face the opposite outcome; the verse marks the other side of the measure.
The light-scaled person’s destination is the abyss; this names the adverse place.
The abyss is identified as a blazing Fire; this completes the measured division with the adverse destination named in the section.
